product.name: Spendwise
product.vision: A Finance Lite backend that lets an individual manage accounts, record transactions, categorize spending, set budgets, transfer money atomically, handle recurring transactions, import CSV statements, auto-apply categorization rules, and view a dashboard/report — built incrementally from a pure-Java domain to a production backend, with optional AI acting only as an advisory layer.
outOfScope: support for every bank file format

releases.title: Java Domain
releases.problem: Spendwise has no domain yet; there is no safe way to represent money, accounts, or transactions, and financial invariants (valid amount/type/account) are unprotected.
releases.goal: Build the core Spendwise domain in pure Java with encapsulated invariants — no Spring, no database, no REST.
acceptanceCriteria: Can create an Account
Can create a Transaction
Basic business invariants are protected inside the domain
Money uses BigDecimal (never double/float for business amounts)
No dependency on Spring, database, or REST

releases.title: Java Application
releases.problem: The domain objects exist but there is no working application around them — no way to store, search, aggregate, or persist transactions between runs.
releases.goal: Turn the domain into a small working Java application with an in-memory repository, transaction service, basic statistics, and simple CSV read/write.
acceptanceCriteria: Can manage transactions in memory
Can search transactions
Can group by category and total income/expense
Can save/load simple data via CSV
Concurrency applied only when a natural use case exists (not forced)

releases.title: Spring Boot Core
releases.problem: The Java application wires its own dependencies manually and cannot grow into a real backend without an application container and configuration.
releases.goal: Migrate the application onto Spring Boot with IoC/DI-managed service and repository beans, reusing the existing domain unchanged.
acceptanceCriteria: Application boots on Spring Boot
Existing Java domain is reused, not rewritten
Business logic is not rewritten just because of the Spring migration
Beans are managed via IoC/DI

releases.title: REST API
releases.problem: Spendwise can only be driven from code/CLI; there is no HTTP surface for creating accounts, recording transactions, or managing categories.
releases.goal: Expose Spendwise over an HTTP REST API with DTOs, bean validation, and consistent error responses.
acceptanceCriteria: Can create an account via HTTP
Can create, list and filter transactions via HTTP
Can manage categories via HTTP
Inputs validated via DTO + Bean Validation
Errors returned consistently (ProblemDetail / RFC 7807)
Frontend not yet required (Swagger/Postman usable)

releases.title: Persistence
releases.problem: Restarting the application loses all data, and transfers between two accounts can leave balances inconsistent if only one side succeeds.
releases.goal: Persist financial data in PostgreSQL via Spring Data JPA and make account transfer atomic with rollback on failure.
acceptanceCriteria: Data survives application restart
Transfer (Account A -500000 / Account B +500000) is atomic
An incomplete/invalid transfer rolls back entirely

releases.title: Security & Ownership
releases.problem: The API is open: any caller can read or modify any account, transaction, or budget — Spendwise is not a real multi-user backend.
releases.goal: Make Spendwise a proper multi-user backend with register/login/JWT authentication and backend-enforced resource ownership.
acceptanceCriteria: Register/login issue JWT and protected endpoints require it
Ownership is checked on the backend, not the frontend
User A cannot read/update/delete User B's Account, Transaction, or Budget

releases.title: Business Engine
releases.problem: Spendwise is still essentially CRUD; it lacks the budgeting, recurring, and rule logic that make it an actual finance product.
releases.goal: Push Spendwise beyond CRUD with Budget, Recurring Transaction, a Rule engine, and advanced statistics via domain services.
acceptanceCriteria: Budget computes limit / spent / remaining / percentage / status per category+period
Budget overrun does not delete or edit real transactions
Recurring transaction has next due date, frequency, active status and avoids duplicates
Rule engine applies categorization by conditions/actions/priority
Advanced statistics/aggregation available

releases.title: Data Processing
releases.problem: Users cannot bring real statement data in; importing the same CSV twice would create uncontrolled duplicates and failures could leave the system in an unclear state.
releases.goal: Process real transaction data via CSV import with an ImportBatch, validation, deduplication, an import result, optional background import for large datasets, and CSV export.
acceptanceCriteria: Import reports successful, duplicate, and failed rows
Importing the same transaction multiple times does not create uncontrolled duplicates
Import failure does not leave the system in an unclear state
CSV export is available
Large datasets can be imported as a background job (optional, 202 Accepted + ImportBatch status)

releases.title: Production Engineering
releases.problem: Dashboard aggregation is recomputed on every request, recurring transactions are not generated automatically, there is no external FX data, and the system lacks tests, observability, and a reproducible environment.
releases.goal: Bring Spendwise close to a production backend: Redis dashboard cache with invalidation, recurring scheduler, external exchange-rate API, testing, OpenAPI, logging, monitoring, and Docker.
acceptanceCriteria: Dashboard aggregation is cached in Redis with correct invalidation
Recurring scheduler runs periodically without creating duplicates
External exchange rate fetched via RestClient/WebClient with retry/failure handling
Unit and integration tests (Testcontainers) pass
Health check and metrics exposed (Actuator/Micrometer)
Application runs in a Dockerized environment

releases.title: Smart Finance
releases.problem: Core functionality needs final stabilization, and there is an opportunity to add valuable intelligent features without letting AI take over business rules.
releases.goal: Stabilize all core functionality and add optional AI category suggestion and monthly insight as an advisory layer, plus portfolio-readiness.
acceptanceCriteria: All core features stable
AI category suggestion only suggests; user confirms before data changes
AI monthly insight turns backend-aggregated numbers into natural language (LLM does not query DB or compute business numbers)
AI never transfers money, edits transactions/budgets, or deletes data
Portfolio README, final demo, and test coverage delivered

buildSteps.title: Write the failing test for Money construction at scale 2
buildSteps.intent: Locks the precision contract before implementation - construction must normalize to scale 2 HALF_UP, and no double may ever build a Money.

buildSteps.title: Implement immutable Money with add/subtract over BigDecimal
buildSteps.intent: The value object every amount in the system flows through; immutability keeps arithmetic safe to share.
buildSteps.doneWhen: Money is immutable, backed by BigDecimal scale 2, add/subtract exact, and no double/float constructor exists
buildSteps.commonMistake: Accepting a double constructor 'for convenience' - one caller away from reintroducing the bug the type exists to kill.

buildSteps.title: Make monetary equality compareTo-based and reject cross-currency arithmetic
buildSteps.intent: BigDecimal.equals treats 0.50 and 0.5 as different; monetary equality must not. Currencies must not mix silently.
buildSteps.doneWhen: new Money("0.50") equals new Money("0.5") via the type's equality, and adding two Money of different currencies throws
buildSteps.mentorHint: Point at compareTo vs equals on the Javadoc - do not write the compare method for the learner.

milestones.name: Java Foundation
milestones.summary: A solid pure-Java domain and a small working application with in-memory storage, statistics, and basic CSV I/O — no framework yet.

milestones.name: Spring App with Persistent API
milestones.summary: The domain runs on Spring Boot, is exposed over a validated REST API, and persists to PostgreSQL with atomic transfers.

milestones.name: Multi-user Product & Data Processing
milestones.summary: Spendwise becomes a real multi-user product: security/ownership, business engine (budget/recurring/rules), and CSV import with deduplication.

milestones.name: Production & Smart Finance
milestones.summary: Production engineering (cache, scheduler, external FX, testing, monitoring, Docker) plus final stabilization and optional advisory AI.

architectureStages.title: Pure Java domain
architectureStages.rationale: Establish encapsulated financial invariants in plain Java before any framework, DB, or transport.

architectureStages.title: Layered Java application (in-memory + file)
architectureStages.changesFromPrev: Added service, generic repository abstraction, statistics, and CSV read/write around the domain.
architectureStages.rationale: Make the domain usable as an application with search, aggregation, and simple persistence.

architectureStages.title: Spring Boot container
architectureStages.changesFromPrev: Beans and configuration now managed by Spring IoC/DI; domain reused unchanged.
architectureStages.rationale: Introduce an application container so the project can grow into a real backend without rewriting business logic.

architectureStages.title: REST API over the service layer
architectureStages.changesFromPrev: Added Spring MVC controllers, DTOs, validation, and a global exception handler.
architectureStages.rationale: Expose Spendwise over HTTP so it can be exercised via Swagger/Postman.

architectureStages.title: JPA persistence on PostgreSQL
architectureStages.diagram: HTTP -> Controller -> Service -> Spring Data JPA -> PostgreSQL
architectureStages.changesFromPrev: Replaced in-memory repository with JPA entities/repositories and added @Transactional atomic transfer.
architectureStages.rationale: Data must survive restart and transfers must be atomic with rollback.

architectureStages.title: Secured multi-user backend
architectureStages.diagram: HTTP -> JWT Filter -> Controller -> Service (ownership) -> JPA -> PostgreSQL
architectureStages.changesFromPrev: Added Spring Security JWT authentication and backend ownership enforcement.
architectureStages.rationale: Each user must only access their own data; protection cannot rely on the frontend.

architectureStages.title: Business engine domain services
architectureStages.diagram: HTTP -> Controller -> Domain Services (Budget/Recurring/Rule) -> JPA -> PostgreSQL
architectureStages.changesFromPrev: Added budget, recurring, and rule-engine domain services with aggregation queries.
architectureStages.rationale: Move Spendwise beyond CRUD into real product behavior.

architectureStages.title: CSV import pipeline
architectureStages.diagram: Upload CSV -> Import API -> ImportBatch -> Parser -> Validate -> Dedup -> JPA -> PostgreSQL (async optional: 202 -> job -> batch status)
architectureStages.changesFromPrev: Added an ImportBatch-driven parse/validate/dedup pipeline and optional async processing.
architectureStages.rationale: Ingest real statement data idempotently without corrupting state.

architectureStages.title: Production backend
architectureStages.diagram: Client -> Spring Boot [PostgreSQL | Redis cache | Scheduler | External FX API] + Actuator/Metrics (Docker)
architectureStages.changesFromPrev: Added Redis dashboard cache, recurring scheduler, external FX integration, tests, monitoring, and Docker.
architectureStages.rationale: Make the application performant, observable, and reproducible like a production backend.

architectureStages.title: Smart finance (advisory AI)
architectureStages.diagram: Client -> Spring Boot REST -> Services -> JPA -> PostgreSQL (+Redis/Scheduler/FX) -> AI suggestion layer (advisory)
architectureStages.changesFromPrev: Added an advisory AI layer for category suggestion and monthly insight on top of the stable core.
architectureStages.rationale: Add intelligent features without letting AI query the DB or override business rules.

day-01.projectProblem: Spendwise represents monetary amounts and must never lose precision or silently overflow. The choice of numeric type (BigDecimal, not double) and the primitive-vs-nullable-wrapper distinction is the technical foundation of the Money value object.
day-01.context: Spendwise xử lý tiền, nên cách biểu diễn số quyết định tính đúng đắn của toàn hệ thống. Bài học này giải thích vì sao tiền phải dùng BigDecimal (khởi tạo từ String, so sánh bằng compareTo) thay vì double, và khi nào một field nên là wrapper cho phép null thay vì primitive.
day-01.application: Dùng trong Spendwise ở release V0.1 Java Domain khi xây kiểu giá trị Money: chọn BigDecimal cho số tiền, so sánh bằng compareTo, và dùng wrapper cho các trường/cột có thể NULL để phân biệt 'chưa có dữ liệu' với giá trị 0.

day-02.context: Bài nền tảng về toán tử, độ ưu tiên, ba nhóm câu lệnh điều khiển luồng, switch statement/expression và vòng lặp theo chuẩn Java 17 — kiến thức ngôn ngữ chung, chưa xây trực tiếp tính năng Spendwise nào.

day-03.context: Lab luyện tập cài đặt StringCalculator (phân tích biểu thức cộng/trừ từ chuỗi) để áp dụng tính bất biến của String và tối ưu bằng kiểu nguyên thủy — bài tập ngôn ngữ chung, không gắn với tính năng Spendwise.

day-04.projectProblem: Spendwise domain objects (Account, Money, Category) must protect their invariants — a balance cannot go negative, a value object cannot exist half-built — so they need private fields, a validating constructor, and meaningful behaviour instead of open setters.
day-04.context: V0.1 của Spendwise là tầng domain thuần Java: các lớp như Account và Money phải luôn ở trạng thái hợp lệ. Bài học này dạy đóng gói (field private + constructor xác thực dữ liệu, không phơi setter công khai) — chính là kỹ thuật để xây các lớp đó.
day-04.application: Dùng trong Spendwise ở release V0.1 Java Domain khi xây Account/Money: field private final, constructor kiểm tra dữ liệu (ví dụ số dư/số tiền không âm), chỉ phơi hành vi có nghĩa (deposit/withdraw) thay vì setBalance; dùng record cho các DTO bất biến chỉ mang dữ liệu.

day-05.projectProblem: Spendwise's business engine needs pluggable rules/policies (auto-categorization, budget/discount policies) that can be added without editing existing code. Polymorphism plus the Strategy pattern is precisely that mechanism.
day-05.context: Bài học này dạy đa hình và abstract class; ở phần thiết kế giới thiệu mẫu Strategy — đóng gói mỗi cách xử lý thành một lớp và chọn hành vi bằng cách chọn object. Đây là nền tảng cho engine luật nghiệp vụ của Spendwise ở release sau.
day-05.application: Sẽ dùng trong Spendwise ở release V0.7 Business Engine: mỗi luật/chính sách là một implementation của một interface chung (như DiscountPolicy trong bài), tầng gọi chỉ phụ thuộc hợp đồng — thêm luật mới không phải sửa code cũ (Open/Closed).

day-06.context: Assignment tổng hợp OOP (Employee/Developer/Manager/PayrollService/EmployeeDTO) để luyện abstract class, kế thừa, polymorphism động và record — bài tập thực hành chung, không xây tính năng Spendwise.

day-07.projectProblem: Spendwise should depend on a Repository abstraction (an interface) rather than a concrete storage class, so persistence can change without touching business logic; and fixed domain sets (transaction/account status/type) should be modeled as enums rather than magic strings.
day-07.context: Bài học này dạy interface như 'hợp đồng' API và nguyên tắc Dependency Inversion (module nghiệp vụ phụ thuộc vào abstraction, không vào lớp cụ thể), cùng enum cho các tập giá trị cố định. Đây là nền tảng cho tầng repository của Spendwise.
day-07.application: Được dùng ngay trong Spendwise ở release V0.2 Java Application khi định nghĩa Repository dưới dạng interface: tầng nghiệp vụ phụ thuộc vào abstraction còn implementation lưu trữ được nối vào ở tầng cấu hình; enum dùng cho các trạng thái/loại cố định của domain (và về sau map bằng @Enumerated(STRING)).

day-08.projectProblem: Spendwise's V0.2 repository, service and CSV layers are built from generics, the Collections Framework and exception handling - techniques this lesson teaches but which own no single task by themselves; the tasks that consume them are task-repository-interface and task-csv-read-write, mapped on day-07 and day-11.
day-08.context: Core Java language foundation — generics, the Collections Framework, the exception hierarchy and try-with-resources — that every later Spendwise layer relies on but which builds no feature by itself.
day-08.application: Dùng trực tiếp trong Spendwise V0.2: generic Repository<T, ID> trên bộ sưu tập, try-with-resources cho đọc/ghi CSV, và xử lý exception khi parse dữ liệu người dùng — nền tảng cho task-repository-interface và task-csv-read-write (map ở day-07 và day-11).

day-09.context: A practice lab re-implementing an ArrayList, a HashMap and a data-access exception hierarchy from scratch to consolidate Day 8 — generic skill-building, not a Spendwise feature.

day-10.projectProblem: Spendwise needs to summarise transactions — total and count of spending grouped by category — which is exactly what a Stream + Collectors.groupingBy pipeline with a BigDecimal reduce sum computes over the in-memory domain (summingDouble is type-incompatible with BigDecimal money — R1).
day-10.context: The Stream API — filter, map, and Collectors.groupingBy for the grouping half, with a BigDecimal reduce for the money sum — is the engine used to compute Spendwise's spending statistics over transactions.
day-10.application: Used in Spendwise to build the V0.2 statistics feature: grouping transactions by category and summing amounts with a Stream collector pipeline.

day-11.projectProblem: Spendwise's CSV import must read potentially large transaction files line-by-line safely (explicit charset, resource closing, path-traversal defence), which is exactly what java.nio.file Path/Files + Files.lines provide.
day-11.context: The NIO.2 File I/O half of this lesson (Path/Files, Files.lines, charset and path-traversal safety) is the foundation for Spendwise's later CSV import; the concurrency half is general JVM knowledge.
day-11.application: Used in Spendwise later (V0.8 Data Processing) to read uploaded CSV transaction files with Files.lines and safe path handling for the import feature.

day-12.projectProblem: Reading a large CSV, filtering invalid rows, aggregating revenue by category and exporting a report is the same shape as Spendwise's bulk CSV transaction import and category reporting.
day-12.context: An assignment building an end-to-end CSV-to-report pipeline (read 500K rows with Files.lines, filter/group/aggregate/top-10, export JSON) — the same skills Spendwise's later CSV import will need.
day-12.application: Used in Spendwise later (V0.8 Data Processing) as the skill basis for reading and aggregating uploaded CSV transaction files; the groupingBy/summingDouble step also mirrors the V0.2 statistics aggregation.

day-13.projectProblem: Migrating Spendwise from plain Java to Spring Boot requires understanding the IoC container, bean scopes and stereotype annotations so the domain/service/repository layers become container-managed beans.
day-13.context: Spring Boot's IoC container, bean scopes and stereotype annotations are the mechanism by which Spendwise's services and repositories become container-managed when it migrates to Spring Boot.
day-13.application: Used in Spendwise's V0.3 Spring Boot Core migration: wiring services/repositories as stateless @Service/@Repository singleton beans managed by the ApplicationContext.

day-14.projectProblem: Spendwise's Spring Boot version must wire its beans correctly — constructor injection for required collaborators, @Configuration/@Bean for third-party objects, and externalised configuration — to stay maintainable and testable.
day-14.context: Constructor injection, @Configuration/@Bean and externalised configuration are how Spendwise's Spring Boot services are wired together and configured after the migration.
day-14.application: Used in Spendwise's V0.3 Spring Boot Core migration: constructor-injecting collaborators into services with final fields and declaring third-party/config beans via @Configuration.

day-15.context: An assignment that practices Spring configuration and DI patterns by building a standalone multi-module Notification Service (Email/SMS/Push) — general Spring skill-building, not a Spendwise feature.

day-16.projectProblem: Spendwise needs HTTP endpoints for each resource - accounts, transactions, categories - with correct REST semantics (status codes, path/query params, JSON bodies), one leaf per resource so a task cannot be partially done.
day-16.context: The core REST controller lesson: @RestController, HTTP-method mappings, path/query binding, and ResponseEntity — the exact building blocks of Spendwise's API layer.
day-16.application: Used in Spendwise to build one controller per resource (account, transaction, category) returning correct status codes (201 + Location on create, 204 on delete) and JSON DTOs rather than raw entities.

day-17.projectProblem: Spendwise must reject invalid request payloads (blank fields, bad amounts) and return a single, consistent error format across all endpoints instead of ad-hoc error bodies.
day-17.context: Building on the Day 16 controllers, this lesson adds input validation (@Valid, custom validators) and centralized error handling (@RestControllerAdvice + ProblemDetail) — the request-hardening layer of the Spendwise API.
day-17.application: Used in Spendwise to validate incoming request DTOs and to funnel all API errors through a global @RestControllerAdvice that returns standardized ProblemDetail responses.

day-18.context: A hands-on lab that consolidates the Day 16-17 REST/validation skills by building a standalone User & Task Management API (CRUD Task with status transitions) — generic practice, not a Spendwise feature.

day-19.projectProblem: Spendwise must persist its domain (accounts, transactions, categories) as JPA entities with correct relationships, cascade rules, and fetch strategies so data is stored and navigated correctly.
day-19.context: This lesson teaches JPA entity mapping and relationships — how to turn Spendwise's domain objects into persisted @Entity classes with the right @ManyToOne/@OneToMany wiring, cascade, and lazy loading.
day-19.application: Used in Spendwise to map Account, Transaction, and Category as JPA entities with correct owning-side relationships, composition cascade/orphanRemoval, and lazy fetching to avoid N+1.

day-20.projectProblem: Spendwise must list transactions with safe pagination/sorting and guarantee that multi-step money operations (e.g. transfers) either fully commit or fully roll back.
day-20.context: This lesson covers advanced repositories (pagination/sorting), transaction management with @Transactional, and auditing — the query and consistency guarantees behind Spendwise's transaction data.
day-20.application: Used in Spendwise to page/sort transaction lists and to wrap money-moving operations in @Transactional so a failure rolls back atomically; optimistic locking (@Version) is optional hardening for concurrent edits.

day-21.projectProblem: Spendwise's V0.5 schema (tables, constraints, money columns) must be created by versioned migrations and validated against the entities — the Flyway/UNIQUE/SUM practice in this assignment is exactly the technique behind task-flyway-baseline, whose build CTA this lesson carries, and task-user-migration, which arrives later in V0.6.
day-21.context: An assignment that consolidates the Day 19-20 persistence skills by building a standalone E-Commerce data layer (5 entities, business queries, Flyway, @DataJpaTest) — generic practice, not the Spendwise schema.
day-21.application: Kỹ thuật dùng trực tiếp trong Spendwise V0.5: Flyway migration owns the schema (R26), single-column inline UNIQUE như corpus dạy, và SUM aggregate cho báo cáo — thực thi qua task-flyway-baseline (build CTA ở day-21), không xây schema E-Commerce trong bài.

day-22.projectProblem: Spendwise is still effectively single-user with no login; it must become a real multi-user backend where each person registers, signs in, passwords are stored safely, and every owned row gains a user_id.
day-22.context: Spendwise has no authentication yet. Today's stateless JWT authentication and secure password hashing are what turn it into a multi-user backend where users can register and sign in.
day-22.application: Used in Spendwise V0.6 (Security & Ownership) to build register/login security primitives (DelegatingPasswordEncoder, stateless filter chain) and the versioned user_id migration that scoping and ownership are built on. Token issuance is NOT here: day-24 owns the TokenIssuer seam and canonical signing executes after day-36.

day-23.projectProblem: Spendwise must guarantee User A cannot read or modify User B's accounts, transactions, or budgets, and must correctly decide CSRF handling for its stateless JWT API.
day-23.context: Now that users can log in, Spendwise must enforce that each user only touches their own data. Method-level authorization (@PreAuthorize) plus correct CSRF handling deliver that ownership guarantee.
day-23.application: Used in Spendwise V0.6 to enforce resource ownership with @PreAuthorize/SpEL and to disable CSRF safely for the Bearer-token API; the N+1 material is the performance foundation reused later for dashboard/query optimization (V0.9).

day-24.projectProblem: Spendwise needs a complete, working auth service (register/login/refresh/logout with early token revocation) plus role- and owner-based access control and performant list queries. Token issuance runs through the TokenIssuer seam here; the canonical NimbusJwtEncoder implementation is task-canonical-token-issuer, scheduled AFTER day-36 — never during the capstone window.
day-24.context: This lab assembles Spendwise's full authentication service and ownership checks end to end, wiring register/login/refresh/logout and role-based access into a working secured backend.
day-24.application: Used in Spendwise V0.6 to ship the end-to-end Auth Service (login flow via the TokenIssuer interface, logout/revocation via blacklist, @PreAuthorize role and owner checks) and to remove N+1 from list endpoints via JOIN FETCH/@EntityGraph. The canonical NimbusJwtEncoder issuer is deliberately NOT built here: task-canonical-token-issuer executes after day-36.

day-25.projectProblem: Spendwise recomputes expensive dashboard/spending aggregations on every request; large imports should not block the request thread, and recurring transactions need periodic processing.
day-25.context: Spendwise's dashboard recomputes spending aggregates on every request, which is costly. Caching backed by Redis, plus async and scheduled processing, is how those hot reads and background jobs get optimized.
day-25.application: Used in Spendwise V0.9 to cache dashboard/category aggregations in Redis with TTL and eviction on writes; the @Async and @Scheduled concepts introduced here back async imports (V0.8) and the recurring-transaction scheduler (V0.9).

day-26.projectProblem: Spendwise users import bank statements as CSV (upload, parse, export) and the app needs foreign-exchange rates from an external service that may be slow or fail.
day-26.context: Spendwise needs to ingest bank-statement CSV files and fetch exchange rates from an outside service. Safe file upload/CSV handling and resilient external API calls are the techniques that unlock both.
day-26.application: MultipartFile upload and CSV escaping underpin Spendwise's V0.8 CSV import/export (feat-import); WebClient plus Retry/Circuit Breaker underpin the V0.9 external exchange-rate integration (feat-exchange-rate).

day-27.context: This is a generic e-commerce practice assignment (product listing, orders, payment gateway) that consolidates the Unit 9 techniques on a non-Spendwise domain, so it maps to no Spendwise feature.

day-28.context: Foundational testing tooling (JUnit 5, Spring Boot slice and integration tests) that will safeguard Spendwise's financial correctness later, but is a general engineering practice rather than a distinct Spendwise feature.

day-29.projectProblem: Once Spendwise runs in production you cannot attach a debugger: you must be able to answer 'is the app healthy' and 'what happened to this request'. This needs structured logs, health checks and metrics.
day-29.context: Khi Spendwise chạy trên production, bạn cần biết ứng dụng có còn khỏe không và điều gì đã xảy ra với mỗi request. Bài này dạy structured logging + MDC, HealthIndicator/Actuator và tài liệu API tự sinh — nền tảng observability cho release V0.9.
day-29.application: Dùng trong Spendwise ở V0.9 (Production Engineering) để bật structured JSON logging + MDC (traceId), viết HealthIndicator kiểm tra database, giới hạn expose Actuator an toàn, và sinh tài liệu OpenAPI cho API.

day-30.projectProblem: Spendwise must reach production readiness: packaged as a reproducible Docker image, observable via health/metrics/logs, and verified against a real database rather than H2.
day-30.context: Lab tổng hợp đưa một ứng dụng đạt chuẩn 'production readiness': đóng gói layered-jar Docker + docker-compose, hoàn thiện observability (Actuator/metrics/HealthIndicator + structured logging) và test hai tầng với Testcontainers — chính là các bước Spendwise cần cho V0.9.
day-30.application: Dùng trong Spendwise ở V0.9 (Production Engineering) để đóng gói image layered-jar, chạy phụ thuộc (DB/Redis) qua docker-compose, hoàn thiện observability và kiểm thử tích hợp bằng Testcontainers với database thật.

day-31.context: Buổi kickoff dự án capstone thương mại điện tử: thống nhất kiến trúc package-per-module, luồng DispatcherServlet và bản API contract trước khi code — kỹ năng thiết kế hệ thống dùng chung, không xây tính năng Spendwise nào.

day-32.context: Hoàn thiện thiết kế database (ERD), chiến lược xử lý lỗi toàn cục và quy ước git workflow cho dự án capstone e-commerce — kỹ năng thiết kế/quy trình chung, không gắn với tính năng Spendwise cụ thể.

day-33.projectProblem: Day 33 unlocks the canonical JWT issuance knowledge Spendwise's final auth task needs (NimbusJwtEncoder + ImmutableSecret + JwtClaimsSet, secret >= 32 bytes UTF-8). Spendwise implementation is scheduled AFTER day-36: the learner should NOT build the Spendwise issuer (task-canonical-token-issuer) during the graded capstone lesson.
day-33.context: Sprint 1 của dự án capstone e-commerce: hiện thực entity, quan hệ cascade, cấu hình JWT Resource Server và Category CRUD — áp dụng lại kiến thức đã học vào một dự án riêng, không xây tính năng Spendwise.
day-33.application: Day 33 unlocks the canonical JWT issuance knowledge (NimbusJwtEncoder/JwtClaimsSet/short-secret-fails-at-encode) that Spendwise's task-canonical-token-issuer requires. That task is scheduled AFTER day-36, in the self-study roadmap — the learner should NOT build the Spendwise issuer during the graded capstone lesson. Discoverability runs task -> lesson via the task's relevantLessonIds, never through a build CTA here.

day-34.context: Sprint 2 của dự án capstone e-commerce: Product CRUD, upload ảnh, thiết kế Cart và caching cho Category/Product — thực hành trong dự án riêng, không xây tính năng Spendwise.
